title: N1.4: [CRITICAL] Remove arbitrary 3000-char truncation in LLM lint rules
description:
All three LLM lint rules silently truncate page content to 3000 characters before sending to the LLM:

```python
# factual-consistency, clarity-score both do:
f"Page: {node.title}\n\n{node.content[:3000]}'

# coverage-gap does:
f"- {n.title}: {(n.content or '')[:200]}"
```

**Why this is critical:**
1. This is classic AI-slop — a hardcoded magic number with no justification or config
2. It silently drops content, meaning lint will MISS issues in the last N chars of any page > 3000 chars
3. It's nearly impossible to discover in production — no warning, no log, just silently wrong results
4. It biases LLM judgments toward the beginning of documents

**Proposed fix:**
- Use `LLMClient.complete(max_tokens=...)` with a token budget instead of char slicing
- Or chunk long content into multiple LLM calls and merge results  
- At minimum, log a WARNING when content is truncated so it's discoverable
- Add a `--llm-context-budget` CLI flag so users control the trade-off
- The 200-char limit in coverage-gap is especially aggressive — a page summary that short will miss most content
close_reason: Replaced hardcoded [:3000] with configurable --llm-context-budget (default 100K), WARNING logged on truncation

title: N1: Compile lint rules (structural + LLM-powered)
description:
Add built-in compile lint rules that check the compiled wiki for structural and semantic quality issues.

**Design:**

Two categories of lint rules:

**Structural rules (deterministic, zero LLM cost):**
1. `broken-wikilinks` — `[[wikilinks]]` that don't resolve to any existing page
2. `orphaned-pages` — pages with no incoming wikilinks from other pages
3. `empty-pages` — concept/entity pages with no body content
4. `stale-summaries` — pages whose source files have changed since last compile (hash mismatch)
5. `duplicate-concepts` — two or more pages about the same concept
6. `missing-frontmatter` — pages without required YAML frontmatter fields
7. `index-sync` — pages not listed in the auto-generated index
8. `citation-integrity` — `^[source.md]` markers pointing to non-existent files

**Semantic rules (optional LLM-powered, opt-in via `--deep`):**
9. `contradictions` — claims in one page that contradict claims in another
10. `claim-verification` — LLM checks if each cited claim is actually supported by the source
11. `summary-accuracy` — LLM checks if the summary accurately reflects the page content

```bash
knox lint                          # Structural rules only (default)
knox lint --deep                   # Structural + LLM-powered rules (~3 LLM calls)
knox lint --fix                    # Auto-fix structural issues (broken links, orphans, frontmatter)
knox lint --pass contradictions    # Run a single rule only
knox lint --json                   # Machine-readable output (for CI)
knox lint --threshold 80           # Exit with error if health score below threshold
```

Output: a `lint-YYYY-MM-DD.md` page in `wiki/lint/` with findings, or JSON with `--json`.

Lint auto-runs at end of compile by default; configurable via `compiler.auto_lint: true/false` in config.

**How to test:**
- Unit tests for each structural rule: create a wiki with known issues, run lint, verify each is caught
- Test `--fix` on broken wikilinks: create page [[missing]], run lint --fix, verify link removed or page created
- Test `--deep` with a mock LLM that returns contradiction findings
- Test `--json` output schema
- Test `--threshold` exit codes (above threshold = 0, below = 1)
- Test `--pass <rule>` runs only that rule
- Test auto-run after compile (with `auto_lint: true`)
- Integration test: compile a corpus, run lint structural, verify no false positives on clean wiki

**What to document:**
- `docs/guides/lint.md`: full rule reference, example output, CI integration
- CLI `--help` for `knox lint`
- FAQ: "Why does lint say I have broken wikilinks?" / "How to add custom lint rules?"
- Example: putting lint in CI pipeline with `--threshold 80 --json`
close_reason: Closed

title: Q12: LLM failover chain (primary → fallback models on failure)
description:
Currently every LLM call site in KNOX has its own ad-hoc `try/except`. On failure, the resolver / WiCER compiler / graph compiler silently drops the chunk (`LLMResolver`), generates dummy probes (`_fallback_probes`), or returns canned dummy probes (`_fallback_evaluate`). That is **not** a real fallback: a 24h corpus ingest that hits rate limits, context-window overflows, or a provider outage will degrade quality to zero without any retry or alternative model.

**Problem (current call sites)**

- `LLMResolver` (`src/knox/resolution/llm.py`): `except` → `ResolvedChunk(chunk=chunk)` passthrough
- `WiCER` (`src/knox/compilation/wicer.py`): `_try_litellm` → `None` → `_fallback_probes` / `_fallback_evaluate` (heuristic-only output)
- `GraphCompiler` (`src/knox/compilation/graph.py`): no LLM call yet, but planned
- `VLMEnricher` (`src/knox/resolution/vlm_enricher.py`): silent failure
- `PipelineConfig` has one `(llm_model, llm_provider)` pair (`src/knox/core/pipeline.py:30-31`)

**Prior art (do not reinvent)**

- **LiteLLM Router** (https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/routing): already used transitively. Supports multiple model groups, cooldown periods, retry policy, and per-call fallback config. Built-in.
- **hermes-agent (MentatBot)**: ordered model list with circuit-breaker
- **opencode**: `primary + fallback[]` per session
- **Portkey gateway**: similar feature set at the proxy layer
- The **sage-wiki** reference does NOT do failover, only per-task routing; we can do both

**Proposed design (lean, not a new framework)**

1. Centralise the LLM call into a single helper module: `src/knox/llm/client.py` with `LiteLLMRouterClient` that wraps `litellm.Router`.
2. Add `llm_fallback_chain: list[str]` to `PipelineConfig` — e.g. `["openai/gpt-4o", "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4", "ollama/llama3.2"]`.
3. Add `llm_fallback_cooldown_seconds: int` (default 60) and `llm_fallback_max_retries_per_model: int` (default 2).
4. Replace the 4-5 `try/except` blocks with: `client.complete(messages, role=...)` which handles chain routing + retries + circuit-breaking internally.
5. Per call site, distinguish TRANSIENT failures (rate limit, timeout, 5xx → retry / next model) from PERMANENT failures (bad prompt, content policy → surface error).
6. Final fallback: structured empty result (current behaviour) but with structured logging that records WHICH model in the chain succeeded/failed and WHY.

**Acceptance criteria**

- One shared LLM call site (no more inline `litellm.completion` in business modules)
- Configurable ordered list of models; failures cascade to next
- Transient vs permanent failure classification
- Per-tier logging: `model_used`, `attempts`, `total_latency_s`
- Test: mock primary model to raise `RateLimitError` → second model is called and returns a result
- Test: all models raise → final passthrough behaviour preserved (no crash)
- Backwards compat: when `llm_fallback_chain` is empty, behave as single-model with single retry (no behaviour change for current users)
- Decision: do we ship as opt-in (`--llm-fallback-chain`) or always-on with empty default? Default: **opt-in** via flag/env `KNOX_LLM_FALLBACK_CHAIN`

**Open question**

Should we also fall back to deterministic extractors (e.g. a small regex-based NER for entities, simple sentence-shingle for probes) as the last resort in the chain? If yes, the chain is a list of `(Model | "deterministic")` and the deterministic entry is the universal safety net.
notes:
## Improvements from Research (audit 2026-06-07)

### Typed error handling
Instead of bare try/except blocks, adopt a typed error hierarchy as seen in notebooklm-llm-wiki-flow:
-  (rate limit, timeout, 5xx) → retry / next model in chain
-  (bad prompt, content policy, auth) → surface error, no retry
-  (invalid model name, missing API key) → fail fast
This eliminates the pattern of silent fallbacks that mask real problems.

### Testing
- Unit test: each error type raises correctly from LiteLLM exceptions
- Unit test: transient errors trigger retry with backoff
- Unit test: transient errors exhaust chain → permanent error raised
- Unit test: permanent error → no retry, surfaced immediately
- Integration test: mock provider returning 429 → verify retry + next model called
- Integration test: all models in chain raise transient → verify final passthrough + warning
- Integration test: configuration error (bad model name) → fast failure, no retry

### Documentation
- docs/guides/llm-config.md: error types, retry behaviour, failover chain configuration
- docs/guides/llm-config.md: how to interpret 'model_used' and 'attempts' in logs
- FAQ: "Why did the LLM call fail?" / "How do I see which model was used?"
- CLI --help for new --llm-fallback-chain flag
close_reason: LLMClient: default_model required, graceful None handling in all consumers

title: N1.1: Health score should weight errors more than warnings
description:
The current health score is a flat `passes / total` ratio. The original spec called for weighted scoring where errors cost more than warnings.

**Current behavior:** A broken wikilink (ERROR) and a missing frontmatter field (WARNING) both count equally as 1 failure.

**Proposed fix:** Weight by severity — ERROR = 3, WARNING = 2, INFO = 1. The health score becomes `100 * (weighted_passes / weighted_total)`. Or simpler: only count failures, with errors penalized more: `100 - (3 * errors + 1 * warnings)`.

**Impact:** N2 eval harness may depend on a meaningful health score. Fix before wiring eval thresholds into CI.

title: N14: Refactor BaseOutputWriter to use Document model + DocumentRenderer
description:
Refactor `BaseOutputWriter` to use rumdl for canonical Markdown rendering, removing all hand-rolled Markdown string formatting from concrete writers.

**The gap:**
The current `BaseOutputWriter` abstract class defines only `write(wiki, output_dir) -> Path`. Concrete writers like `MarkdownWriter` assemble Markdown via string concatenation with hardcoded formatting (heading prefixes, TOC layout, source links). This approach:

1. **Bleeds format logic into every writer** — `MarkdownWriter._write_toc()`, `MarkdownWriter._write_node()`, etc. would each contain flavor-specific formatting hacks
2. **Makes flavor support expensive** — adding Obsidian support means forking the whole string assembly
3. **Prevents reuse** — other tools (MCP server, JSON output) can't easily render the same content in different flavors

**Design:**

**Phase 1 — Introduce `Document` intermediate model**
Create a `Document` dataclass that separates content from presentation:

```python
@dataclass
class Document:
    """Intermediate representation of a compiled wiki page, flavor-agnostic."""
    title: str
    body: str                         # markdown body with [[wikilinks]]
    frontmatter: dict[str, Any]       # metadata to render as YAML frontmatter
    heading_level: int = 1
    source_chunks: list[SourceChunk] = field(default_factory=list)
    toc_entries: list[TocEntry] = field(default_factory=list)
```

**Phase 2 — `DocumentRenderer` with rumdl backend**
```python
class DocumentRenderer:
    """Renders Document to a specific Markdown flavor via rumdl."""
    
    def __init__(self, flavor: str = "obsidian"):
        self.flavor = flavor
    
    def render(self, doc: Document) -> str:
        """Render document to Markdown string, format via rumdl."""
        raw = self._assemble(doc)       # simple template, no flavor logic
```

title: N13: Multi-flavor Markdown output via rumdl
description:
Use the `rumdl` Python package (https://github.com/rvben/rumdl) for multi-flavor Markdown output instead of writing custom Markdown generation code in output writers.

**The gap:**
The current `MarkdownWriter` assembles Markdown via Python string concatenation — a single format with hardcoded heading levels, wikilinks, and layout. This produces a flat `wiki.md` that only works for basic consumption. Different consumers need different Markdown flavors:

| Consumer | Flavor | Needed adjustments |
|----------|--------|--------------------|
| Obsidian vault | Obsidian | `[[wikilinks]]`, frontmatter, no lint warnings on special syntax |
| GitHub README | GFM | Standard headings, relative links, code fences |
| MkDocs site | MkDocs | Title case headings, `admonition` syntax, nav structure |
| Quarto / RMarkdown | Quarto | Special chunk syntax, bibliography format |
| Jupyter Book / Sphinx | MyST | Role syntax, directive syntax |
| MDX (React docs) | MDX | JSX imports, component syntax |

**Why rumdl instead of custom writers:**
- rumdl supports **10 flavors out of the box** (standard, gfm, mkdocs, mdx, obsidian, pandoc, quarto, kramdown, azure_devops, myst) with auto-detection
- It's a **linter + formatter** — approves syntax and normalizes output per flavor
- Available as a **Python package** (`pip install rumdl` / `uv add rumdl`)
- Written in **Rust** — formatting is near-instant
- The `rumdl fmt` command can read from stdin and write formatted output
- Avoids the maintenance burden of hand-rolling flavor-specific Markdown writers

**Implementation:**
- Add `rumdl` as an optional dependency (`knox[rumdl]`)
- Add `--flavor` / `-f` option to `knox compile` (default: auto-detect from output dir or config)
- In `MarkdownWriter`:
  1. Build canonical Markdown with wikilinks and frontmatter (content is flavor-agnostic)
  2. After writing, pass the output file through `rumdl fmt --flavor <FLAVOR>` for formatting
  3. If rumdl is not installed, fall back to raw output with a warning
- Config file: `output.flavor: obsidian | gfm | mkdocs | quarto | myst | mdx | standard`
- Auto-detection: if output dir contains `.obsidian/` → use Obsidian flavor; if `mkdocs.yml` → use MkDocs; etc.
- Ignored rumdl rules for KNOX-specific syntax (custom frontmatter, `[//]: #` comments, etc.) via `.rumdl.toml`

**Writers affected:**
- `MarkdownWriter` (primary) — gains per-flavor formatting
- `JsonWriter` (unaffected — JSON is flavor-agnostic)
- `TypstWriter` (unaffected — Typst is not Markdown)

**Anti-pattern enforced:**
- **Do NOT write custom Markdown converters.** Use rumdl. If a flavor isn't supported by rumdl, contribute upstream rather than building a local workaround.

**How to test:**
- Unit test: `rumdl fmt --flavor obsidian` on a mock wiki page produces valid Obsidian Markdown
- Unit test: `rumdl fmt --flavor gfm` on the same content produces different (GFM-valid) output
- Unit test: missing `rumdl` package → graceful fallback with warning, no crash
- Integration test: `knox compile --flavor obsidian` → output passes `rumdl check --flavor obsidian`

- Integration test: output dir contains `.obsidian/` → auto-detected as Obsidian flavor

- Edge case: file with `[[wikilinks]]` in GFM flavor → warning or graceful handling

**What to document:**

title: N10: Per-concept prompt budget (fair-share truncation)
description:
Add a configurable character ceiling for the combined source content sent to the LLM per concept, preventing context-window overflow when many sources contribute to the same concept.

**Problem:**
When a popular concept (e.g., "transformer", "attention") appears in 50+ sources, the combined source content can easily exceed the LLM's context window. Without a budget, the compilation either fails with a context-length error or silently degrades.

**Design:**

```yaml
# config.yaml
compiler:
  prompt_budget_chars: 200000       # Character ceiling per concept (~50K tokens)
```

Or via env var: `KNOX_PROMPT_BUDGET_CHARS=200000`

**How it works:**
- When the combined source content for a concept exceeds the budget, truncation activates
- Each contributing source gets a **fair share**: `budget / number_of_sources`
- Sources with more relevant content (as determined by chunk matching) can claim unused budget from less relevant sources
- Truncation happens at chunk boundaries, not mid-chunk
- A warning is printed to stderr: `[budget] concept "transformer": 150K chars from 23 sources, budget 200K, 2 sources truncated`
- The budget applies per concept, not per compile run

**Integration with Q20 (tiered compilation):**
- Budget can vary by tier: tier 3 gets full budget, tier 1 gets smaller budget (summary only)

**Integration with N3 (two-phase compile):**
- During Phase 2 generation, per-concept budget ensures fair allocation across all contributing sources

**How to test:**
- Set budget very low (100 chars) → verify truncation warning printed
- Set budget very high (10M chars) → verify no truncation
- Test fair-share: 4 sources, budget 400 chars → each gets ~100 chars
- Test with unequal relevance: one source highly relevant, three irrelevant → relevant source gets more budget
- Test truncation at chunk boundaries (no mid-chunk cuts)
- Test warning output format (parseable for CI)
- Test default budget (200K) with a large corpus → verify no context overflow
- Integration test: 50 sources all mentioning "transformer" → compile succeeds without overflow

**What to document:**
- `docs/guides/compilation.md`: prompt budget explanation, how fair-share works
- `docs/guides/compilation.md`: tuning budget for different LLMs (8K vs 128K context)
- CLI `--help` for `knox compile` (new `--prompt-budget` flag)

title: N3: Two-phase compile (extract all concepts first, then generate pages)
description:
Restructure the compile pipeline into a true two-phase process: extract all concepts from all sources first, then generate pages.

**Current state:**
KNOX processes sources sequentially through the 5-tier pipeline. Each source is parsed, chunked, resolved, compiled, and written independently. If source A mentions "attention" and source B mentions "self-attention", they produce separate pages — no cross-source merging.

**Two-phase design:**

**Phase 1 — Extraction (all sources)**
- Run T1 (parse) + T2 (chunk) + T3 (resolution, deterministic part) on ALL sources first
- Collect all extracted concepts, entities, relations into a unified candidate pool
- Detect duplicates across sources: same concept mentioned in multiple sources
- Build a merge map: which sources contribute to which concepts
- Catch all failures before any pages are generated
- Output: `.knox/phase1/` — JSON manifest of all candidates with source provenance

**Phase 2 — Generation (per concept)**
- For each unique concept: generate a page using ALL contributing sources as context
- Merge logic: an existing page gets updated (new info appended, no deletion) — not overwritten
- For concepts with many contributors: apply per-concept prompt budget (N10) with fair-share truncation
- Generate comparison pages for concepts that are explicitly compared across sources
- Write `log.md`, `index.md`, provenance metadata

**Benefits:**
- Order-independent: same set of sources produces the same wiki regardless of ingest order
- Cross-source merging: "attention" and "self-attention" from different papers land on one page
- Failure-resilient: Phase 1 completes or rolls back entirely; Phase 2 never gets partial input
- Better LLM context: generation sees all source material at once

**Backwards compatibility:**
- `--single-pass` flag restores old sequential behaviour
- Default mode is two-phase (controlled by `compiler.mode: two-phase` / `single-pass`)

**How to test:**
- Test basic two-phase: compile two sources with overlapping concepts → verify shared page produced
- Test compared to single-pass: same sources, both modes → two-phase should merge, single-pass should not
- Test failure resilience: inject a parse error in one source → Phase 1 fails before Phase 2 starts
- Test merge behavior: re-compile with new source → existing pages updated, not overwritten
- Test with 100+ sources: verify Phase 1 completes, Phase 2 generates all pages
- Test `--single-pass` flag produces same output as current behaviour
- Test per-concept prompt budget truncation (with N10)

title: Q23: External parser subprocess protocol
description:
Add an `ExternalParser` that wraps any executable as a document parser via a stdin/stdout protocol.

**Problem:** KNOX has `BaseParser` implementations for Docling, PdfPlumber, and Pandoc. But users may have domain-specific parsers (proprietary formats, custom extractors, language-specific tools) that don't fit the Python ecosystem. Instead of requiring a Python `BaseParser` subclass, let users write parsers in any language.

**Protocol:**
- stdin: raw file bytes
- stdout: JSON with the same schema as `ParsedDocument`
- stderr: logging (forwarded to KNOX logger)
- Exit code 0: success, non-zero: error

**Configuration:**

```yaml
# config.yaml or parsers.yaml
parsers:
  external: true                  # enable external parser loading
  trust_external: true            # acknowledge unsandboxed execution
  definitions:
    - extensions: [".rtf"]
      command: python3
      args: ["rtf_parser.py"]
      timeout: 30                 # seconds
    - extensions: [".dwg", ".dxf"]
      command: cad-extract
      args: []
      timeout: 120                # max 120s
```

When `parsers.external: false` (default), external parser definitions are ignored. Requires `parsers.trust_external: true` as a separate opt-in as a security acknowledgement.

**Security:**
- Timeout enforcement (30s default, configurable, 120s max)
- Environment stripping (only PATH, HOME, LANG passed through)
- Parsers run as subprocess (no sandbox beyond OS process isolation)
- Double opt-in: `parsers.external` + `parsers.trust_external`
- Network isolation not enforced (we can't do this portably) — documented as a caveat

**Implementation:**
```python
class ExternalParser(BaseParser):
    def __init__(self, command: str, args: list[str], timeout: int):
        self.command = command
        self.args = args
        self.timeout = timeout

    def parse(self, source_path: Path) -> ParsedDocument:
        result = subprocess.run(
            [self.command, *self.args],
            input=source_path.read_bytes(),
            capture_output=True,
            timeout=self.timeout,
        )
        result.check_returncode()
        return ParsedDocument.model_validate_json(result.stdout)
```

**Prior art:** `sage-wiki` external parsers (stdin/stdout protocol), ripgrep's `--type` extensibility, Pandoc's reader system

**Acceptance criteria:**
- `ExternalParser` class implements `BaseParser`
- Registers with `ParserRouter` like any built-in parser via config
- Plugin is auto-discovered from config when `parsers.external: true`
- Timeout enforcement kills subprocess and raises clear error
- Non-zero exit code produces a clear error with stderr content
- stderr from parser forwarded to KNOX logger at DEBUG level
- `parsers.external: false` (default) skips all external definitions silently
- `parsers.trust_external: false` (default) skips even if `external: true`
- Test: a python3 script that reads stdin and writes valid JSON
- Test: timeout kills long-running parser
- Test: non-zero exit + stderr → clear error message
- Test: both opt-in flags required (security)
close_reason: Implemented: ExternalParser (subprocess) and HTTPParser (POST), parser registry, knox list-parsers command

title: Q21: Output trust / grounding verification
description:
Add an output trust system that quarantines query and compilation outputs until they pass grounding verification and consensus checks.

**Problem:** When the LLM answers a query or compiles an article, its output is a claim, not a verified fact. Without safeguards, wrong answers get into the wiki and pollute future queries. The WiCER loop (T4) already does iterative refinement with LLM-as-judge evaluation, but it only runs during compilation — not for ad-hoc queries.

**Design:**

**Phase 1: Quarantine new outputs**
- Query outputs from `knox query` start as "pending" in `wiki/under_review/`
- Compilation outputs that score below a grounding threshold during WiCER are flagged as "draft"
- Draft/pending outputs are excluded from search by default; explicit `--include-drafts` flag to include

**Phase 2: Grounding verification (`knox verify`)**
```bash
knox verify --all                         # Verify all pending outputs
knox verify --since 7d                    # Verify outputs from last 7 days
knox verify --limit 20                    # Verify up to 20 outputs
knox verify attention.md                  # Verify a specific output
```
- Re-uses the WiCER LLM-as-judge evaluate step: for each claim in the output, check if it's entailed by the cited source passages
- Produces a grounding score per output (0.0-1.0)

**Phase 3: Consensus**
- If the same question or compilation is re-run and produces the same answer from different source chunks, confirmations accumulate
- Independence scored via Jaccard distance between chunk sets
- `consensus_threshold: 3` confirmations for auto-promote

**Phase 4: Promotion**
```bash
knox outputs list                              # List by state: pending, confirmed, conflict, stale
knox outputs promote 2026-06-07-attention.md    # Manually promote
knox outputs reject 2026-06-07-attention.md     # Reject and delete
knox outputs resolve 2026-06-07-attention.md    # Promote one, reject conflicts
knox outputs clean --older-than 90d              # Clean up stale
```

```yaml
# config.yaml
trust:
  include_outputs: verified     # "false" (exclude all), "verified" (confirmed only), "true" (legacy)
  consensus_threshold: 3        # confirmations needed for auto-promote
  grounding_threshold: 0.8      # minimum grounding score (0.0-1.0)
  similarity_threshold: 0.85    # cosine similarity for question matching
  auto_promote: true            # auto-promote when all thresholds met
```

**Prior art:** `sage-wiki` output trust system

**Acceptance criteria (Phase 1+2 only, MVPs for Phases 3-4):**
- Query outputs written to `wiki/under_review/` by default
- `--trust` flag on compile: `--trust low` (no check), `--trust medium` (warning only), `--trust high` (block if below threshold)
- `knox verify --all` runs grounding checks on all pending outputs
- Grounding score logged per output
- Outputs below threshold remain excluded from search
- Source changes during compile auto-demote confirmed outputs whose cited sources changed
- `--include-drafts` flag on `knox query` includes pending/draft outputs in search
- `knox outputs list/promote/reject` basic CLI verbs work
- Existing compile tests pass without trust system (behaviour unchanged when config absent)

title: Q20: Tiered compilation (skippable pipeline tiers)
description:
Implement tiered compilation: allow the pipeline to skip expensive tiers for sources that don't need them, auto-promote frequently accessed sources, and auto-demote stale ones.

This is a major scaling feature. KNOX's 5-tier pipeline maps perfectly to sage-wiki's tier system:

| Tier | KNOX Equivalent | What Runs | Cost | Speed |
|------|----------------|-----------|------|-------|
| 0 — Index | T1 (parse) + T5 (output raw) | Parse + store parsed doc | Free | ~5ms |
| 1 — Index + embed | T1 + T2 (chunk) + embed | Parse + chunk + vectorize | ~$0.00002/doc | ~200ms |
| 2 — Code/structure parse | T1 + T3 (deterministic resolve) | Structure summary, no LLM | Free | ~10ms |
| 3 — Full compile | T1+2+3+4+5 (all LLM stages) | Full pipeline | ~$0.05-0.15 | ~5-8min |

**Design:**

```yaml
# config.yaml
compiler:
  default_tier: 3           # default for all sources (3 = full pipeline, same as now)
  tier_defaults:            # per-extension overrides
    json: 0                  # structured data — index only
    yaml: 0
    md: 1                    # prose — index + embed
    py: 2                    # code — parse structure, no LLM
    pdf: 3                   # papers — full compile
  auto_promote: true         # promote to tier 3 based on search hits
  auto_demote: true          # demote stale articles after N days
  promote_threshold: 3       # search hits before auto-promote
  demote_days: 90            # days without queries before demotion
```

**Pipeline changes:**
- Each tier has a `run()` / `skip()` method
- `PipelineConfig.tier: int` controls which tier to execute for the current source
- Tiers are cumulative: tier 2 runs tiers 0+1+2, tier 3 runs all
- Per-source completion state persisted in `.knox/compile_state.db` (SQLite)
- On restart, only sources whose hash changed or whose tier increased are re-processed
- This solves the anti-pattern from sage-wiki issue #88 (resetting all pass flags)

**Compile-on-demand:**
When a search (Q17) finds relevant sources that are at tier < 3, the query response flags them: "Related sources found but not fully compiled. Run `knox compile --promote <source>` to compile them."

**Prior art:** `sage-wiki` tiered compilation, `sage-wiki` auto-promote/auto-demote

**Acceptance criteria:**
- `--tier N` flag on `knox compile` overrides default
- `.knox/compile_state.db` tracks per-source (hash, current_tier, last_compile, search_hits)
- Restarting a compile picks up where it left off (per-source, not from zero)
- `--force` flag re-processes all sources regardless of state
- Auto-promote: after N search hits (N=3 default), source upgrades to tier 3 on next compile
- Auto-demote: source older than D days (D=90 default) without hits → downgraded to tier 1
- `knox status` shows tier distribution (e.g., "Tier 3: 45, Tier 1: 120, Tier 0: 34")
- New tests: tier ordering, state persistence, tier override, auto-promote, auto-demote
- Backwards compat: no config = tier 3 for all (same as current behaviour)

**Anti-pattern to avoid (from sage-wiki #88):**
- Compile state (pass flags, completion markers) resets on process restart
- **Our fix:** persistent SQLite store; only stale/changed sources re-process

Refine from two-phase to three explicit passes:
1. Extraction (thinking mode): LLM reads source, returns structured JSON (summary, entities, concepts, tags)
2. Page drafting (streaming): one call per entity/concept, with merge logic for existing pages

title: Q17: query command (Q&A against compiled wiki)
description:
Add a `knox query` command to ask questions against the compiled wiki.

This is the first "read" use of the compiled wiki output — users can ask natural language questions and get answers grounded in their sources.

**Usage:**

```bash
knox query "what is flash attention?"
knox query "attention mechanisms" --top-k 5
knox query "attention" --format text          # default: plain text answer
knox query "attention" --format json          # structured answer with citations
knox query "attention" --raw                  # just the context chunks, no LLM answer
```

**Architecture (start minimal, grow):**

**Phase 1 (MVP):** Deterministic retrieval
1. Scan compiled articles for token overlap with the query (TF-IDF / simple token match)
2. Return top-k article excerpts as context
3. Optional: pass context to configured LLM for a synthesised answer

**Phase 2 (enhanced):** zvec semantic search (when zvec store is active)
1. Embed the query using configured embed model
2. Cosine-similarity search against chunk vectors
3. RRF fusion with BM25 results (when FTS5 available)

**Phase 3 (graph context):** After Q25 search enhancements land
1. Query expansion via LLM (keywords + semantic rewrites + hyde)
2. LLM re-ranking of top candidates
3. Graph expansion via ontology relations

**Prior art:** `sage-wiki query`, standard RAG Q&A

**Acceptance criteria (MVP):**
- `knox query "question"` returns a text answer with source citations
- `--top-k` controls number of context chunks (default: 5)
- `--raw` returns context chunks without LLM synthesis
- `--format json` returns `{answer, citations: [{article, source, snippet, score}]}`
- Works with no zvec index (fallback to token overlap or skip)
- Graceful degradation: no compiled wiki → clear error message
- Graceful degradation: LLM unavailable → return raw context only with warning

title: Q19: ignore patterns for source scanning
description:
Add `ignore` patterns to the source scanner so users can exclude certain files or directories from being parsed and compiled.

**Usage:**

In config file:
```yaml
sources:
  - path: sources
    type: auto
    recursive: true

ignore:
  - drafts/
  - personal/
  - "*.tmp"
  - temp-*.pdf
```

Patterns are evaluated relative to each source directory. Both file and directory patterns are supported. Glob syntax follows `pathlib.Path.match()` semantics (extended with `**` for recursive matching when `--recursive` is active).

**Design:**
- `resolve_files()` in `_sources.py` gains an optional `ignore_patterns: list[str]` parameter
- Patterns are compiled to `PurePath.match()` predicates
- A file is excluded if its relative path (w.r.t. the source dir being scanned) matches ANY ignore pattern
- When `.knox/config.yaml` is present, patterns from `ignore:` are loaded automatically
- CLI flag: `--ignore PATTERN` repeatable, or `--ignore-file .knoxignore` (gitignore-compatible format)

**Prior art:** `sage-wiki` `ignore:` in config.yaml, `.gitignore` semantics, ripgrep's `.ignore` file

**Acceptance criteria:**
- `resolve_files(..., ignore_patterns=["drafts/"])` excludes everything under `drafts/`
- `resolve_files(..., ignore_patterns=["*.tmp"])` excludes `.tmp` files everywhere
- Patterns relative to source directory work correctly
- Recursive mode respects ignore patterns in subdirectories
- CLI `--ignore` flag repeatable (multiple values)
- `.knoxignore` file auto-discovered when present (gitignore syntax)
- Test: patterns that match nothing don't break anything
- Test: nested ignore (exclude dir but include a specific file inside it — negation with `!`)

title: Q18: Custom frontmatter fields + write command
description:
Allow users to declare custom frontmatter fields that the LLM assesses during compilation, and add a `knox write` command for one-shot article/summary generation from a source.

**Part A — Custom frontmatter fields**

Currently, `CompiledWiki` articles have fixed metadata (concept, aliases, sources, created_at). This feature lets users declare extra LLM-assessed fields in config that get extracted from the LLM's compilation response and added to article YAML frontmatter.

```yaml
# config.yaml
compiler:
  article_fields:
    - language
    - domain
    - difficulty      # beginner / intermediate / advanced
```

Users update their prompts (see customizable prompts in Q15) to include these fields:

```
At the end of your response, state:
Language: (the primary language of the concept)
Domain: (the academic field)
Difficulty: beginner, intermediate, or advanced
Confidence: high, medium, low
```

The pipeline parses these from the LLM response body and merges them into the YAML frontmatter. Ground-truth fields (`concept`, `aliases`, `sources`, `created_at`) remain code-generated and always accurate.

**Part B — `knox write` command**

One-shot article/summary from one or more sources without running the full pipeline:

```bash
knox write summary attention.pdf               # Quick summary of a paper
knox write article attention.pdf               # Full concept article
knox write article attention.pdf --format json # Structured output
knox write article *.pdf --name flash-attention # Write article on a concept from multiple sources
```

Runs a mini-pipeline: parse → chunk → resolve → compile → output, but on a limited set of sources. Useful for quick outputs without waiting for a full corpus compile.

**Prior art:** `sage-wiki write`, `sage-wiki` custom article_fields, custom prompts

**Acceptance criteria (Part A):**
- `compiler.article_fields` in config accepted and validated
- LLM response body parsed for declared fields (case-insensitive key matching)
- Fields merged into article frontmatter YAML
- Missing fields → `null` or `unknown` (not an error)
- Ground-truth fields never overridden by LLM output
- Existing tests pass (no behaviour change when config absent)

**Acceptance criteria (Part B):**
- `knox write summary <path>` runs parse → chunk → LLM summary
- `knox write article <path>` runs parse → chunk → resolve → compile → output
- Multiple source files accepted
- `--name` sets the concept name (otherwise derived from content)
- Output goes to wiki/ (controlled by --output-dir)
- Help output consistent with existing commands

title: Q13: Per-task LLM configuration (different model per pipeline stage)
description:
KNOX has 5 tiers and at least 4 distinct LLM call sites, all currently using a single (llm_model, llm_provider) pair from PipelineConfig. In practice these stages have very different cost/quality profiles:

- Tier 3 LLMResolver: bulk chunk processing, thousands of calls per corpus → wants cheap/fast
- Tier 4 WiCER probes: smaller set, want balanced
- Tier 4 WiCER judge/refine: small set, want high quality
- Tier 3 VLMEnricher: figure analysis → wants vision-capable model
- Embedding: separate concern, may use a different provider

Using one model for all stages either overpays (sonnet for NER) or under-delivers (haiku for article writing). The sage-wiki reference (https://github.com/xoai/sage-wiki#configuration) handles this with a `models: { summarize, extract, write, lint, query }` section in `config.yaml`. We should adopt the same pattern, mapped onto KNOX's own stages.

**Reference (sage-wiki):**

```yaml
models:
  summarize: gemini-3-flash-preview
  extract:   gemini-3-flash-preview
  write:     gemini-3-flash-preview
  lint:      gemini-3-flash-preview
  query:     gemini-3-flash-preview
```

Plus a separate `embed:` section that can use a DIFFERENT provider.

**Proposed design for KNOX**

1. Replace `llm_model` / `llm_provider` on `PipelineConfig` with a structured `LLMProfile` object:

   ```python
   LLMProfile(name: str, provider: str, temperature: float = 0.0, max_tokens: int | None = None)
   ```

2. Per-stage profile map on `PipelineConfig`:
   - `llm_resolve: LLMProfile`        # Tier 3 entity/relation extraction
   - `llm_vlm: LLMProfile`            # Tier 3 figure enrichment
   - `llm_wicer_probe: LLMProfile`
   - `llm_wicer_judge: LLMProfile`
   - `llm_wicer_refine: LLMProfile`

3. Defaults: each stage defaults to the current single model (`ollama/llama3.2`) so behaviour is unchanged for users who don't set this.

4. CLI: new `--llm-profile PATH` flag (TOML/YAML file) and `--llm-resolve MODEL`, `--llm-vlm MODEL`, etc. shorthand flags. The shorthand flags apply per-stage; the file applies wholesale.

5. Env vars: `KNOX_LLM_RESOLVE`, `KNOX_LLM_VLM`, `KNOX_LLM_WICER_PROBE`, `KNOX_LLM_WICER_JUDGE`, `KNOX_LLM_WICER_REFINE`.

6. The shared client from Q12 reads the profile by role:
   - `client.complete(messages, role="resolve")` → uses `llm_resolve`
   - `client.complete(messages, role="vlm")` → uses `llm_vlm`
   - etc.

**Acceptance criteria**

- `LLMProfile` dataclass with name, provider, temperature, max_tokens
- `PipelineConfig` exposes 5 stage-specific profiles
- Single shared `LLMClient` used by all stages (depends on Q12 client)
- CLI supports both `--llm-profile file.yml` and individual `--llm-<stage> <model>` flags
- Env-var binding for each stage
- `--help` shows the per-stage options with sensible defaults
- A `docs/configuration.md` (or `docs/llm-profiles.md`) page showing example profiles: cheap-and-fast ("all haiku"), quality ("all sonnet"), mixed ("resolve=haiku, write=sonnet"), local-only ("all llama3.2")
- Test: setting `--llm-wicer-judge` to a different model results in different `litellm.completion` call args at that stage
- Backwards compat: a single `--llm-model` flag still works as a global override (writes to all 5 profiles)

**Relationship to Q12 (failover)**

The two stack: per-task config selects WHICH model is the primary for a role; failover chain provides a FALLBACK list if the primary fails. A profile entry in the per-stage map can itself be `{primary: "gpt-4o", fallback: ["claude-sonnet-4"]}` or just a single string. description:
Add a schema layer that defines page kinds and compilation rules, making the wiki structure-aware.

**Design:**

An optional `.knox/schema.json` file that declares page kinds, per-kind rules, and seed pages:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "kinds": {
    "concept": {
      "description": "Standalone idea or pattern",
      "minWikilinks": 1,
      "minConfidence": 0.5,
      "allowEmpty": false
    },
    "entity": {
      "description": "Specific person, product, organization, or named artifact",
      "minWikilinks": 1,
      "fields": ["aliases", "category", "external_urls"]
    },
    "comparison": {
      "description": "Side-by-side analysis across concepts or entities",
      "minWikilinks": 3,
      "fields": ["compared_entities", "criteria", "verdict"]
    },
    "overview": {
      "description": "Map page connecting several concepts in a domain",
      "minWikilinks": 5,
      "seedPages": ["index"]
    }
  },
  "defaultKind": "concept",
  "seedPages": ["overview", "index"]
}
```

**How it works:**
- During compile, each generated page is tagged with a `kind` in frontmatter
- Kinds influence prompt templates: a `comparison` page gets a different compile prompt than a `concept`
- Lint rules enforce per-kind requirements: `minWikilinks`, `minConfidence`, required fields
- `seedPages` tells compile to create anchor pages even when no source directly generates them
- Schema is optional; missing or invalid `kind` values fall back to `defaultKind`
- CLI tools: `knox schema init`, `knox schema show`

**Benefits for Q24 (contribution packs):**
Each pack can ship a schema that extends the base schema with domain-specific kinds:

```json
// academic-research pack
{
  "extends": "base",
  "kinds": {
    "finding": {
      "description": "A specific research finding with evidence",
      "minWikilinks": 2,
      "fields": ["evidence_level", "contradicts"]
    }
  }
}
```

**How to test:**
- Test schema parse: valid JSON, invalid JSON, missing fields, extra fields
- Test compile with schema: pages get correct `kind` in frontmatter
- Test compile without schema: all pages default to `concept`
- Test per-kind lint enforcement: comparison with 1 wikilink → warning (min is 3)
- Test `seedPages`: schema with `seedPages: ["overview"]` → overview page generated even with no explicit source
- Test schema extension: academic schema extends base → packs merge kinds
- Test `knox schema init` → writes starter file
- Test `knox schema show` → prints resolved schema (after merges)
- Integration test: compile with academic schema → finding types created

**What to document:**
- `docs/guides/schema.md`: schema format, kinds reference, seed pages, extension
- `docs/guides/schema.md`: example schemas for different domains
- CLI `--help` for `knox schema`
- FAQ: "What page kinds exist?" / "How do I add a custom page kind?"
- Tutorial: "Creating a domain-specific schema"

title: N7: Intent classification for queries
description:
Add intent classification to `knox query` (and `knox chat` if implemented) so casual messages skip expensive retrieval.

**Problem:**
Every query currently goes through the full search pipeline (embedding, LLM reranking, synthesis). Casual messages like "hi", "thanks", "what can you do?" waste ~30s and LLM tokens for no retrieval benefit.

**Design:**

```bash
knox query "hi"                                    # → "Hello! I can answer questions about your wiki..."
knox query "what are the main findings?"            # → Full retrieval + synthesis (normal)
knox query "thanks" --no-classify                   # → Also retrieves (opt-out)
```

**How it works:**
- A lightweight classifier (keyword-based or tiny ML model, no LLM call) runs on every query before retrieval
- Intent categories:
  - `greeting` — "hi", "hello", "hey", "good morning"
  - `gratitude` — "thanks", "thank you", "appreciate it"
  - `help` — "what can you do", "help", "commands"
  - `offtopic` — "how's the weather", "tell me a joke"
  - `knowledge` — anything that looks like a question about the wiki (trigger retrieval)
- Greeting/gratitude/help intents get a quick canned response with a pointer to `--help` or `knox guide`
- Offtopic intents return "I'm a knowledge base assistant. I can answer questions about your compiled wiki."
- Knowledge intents proceed to full retrieval + synthesis
- Classification is **free** (keyword patterns first, optional tiny model later)
- `--no-classify` flag bypasses classification entirely

**Configuration:**

```yaml
# config.yaml
query:
  intent_classification: true      # default: on
  classify_min_length: 3           # skip classification for very short queries (3 chars threshold)
```

**How to test:**
- Test each intent category: greeting → canned response, no retrieval triggered
- Test knowledge query → full retrieval path
- Test `--no-classify` bypasses classification
- Test edge cases: "hi, what is attention?" → should classify as knowledge (has substance)
- Test very short query: "?" → no classification, passes through
- Test offtopic: "tell me a joke" → polite refusal, no retrieval
- Test classification speed (should be <5ms, no LLM call)
- Integration test: mock classifier → verify correct pipeline path triggered

**What to document:**
- `docs/guides/query.md`: intent classification overview, what triggers each response
- CLI `--help` for `knox query` (new `--no-classify` flag)
- FAQ: "Why did KNOX respond without searching my wiki?"

title: N6: 3-way query scope (Wiki / Raw / Hybrid)
description:
Extend `knox query` with three scope modes so users can choose how to retrieve information.

**Design:**

```bash
knox query "attention mechanisms"                       # Default: hybrid (Wiki + Raw)
knox query "attention mechanisms" --scope wiki          # Thematic: only compiled wiki pages
knox query "attention mechanisms" --scope raw           # Exact: only original source documents
knox query "attention mechanisms" --scope hybrid        # Both (default)
knox query "attention mechanisms" --scope wiki --top-k 10
```

**Scope behaviour:**

- **`wiki`** — Search compiled wiki pages (concepts, entities, syntheses). Best for thematic, synthesized answers. Answers cite `[[wikilinks]]` to wiki pages.
- **`raw`** — Search original source documents. Best for exact lookups ("what did the 2023 paper say?"). Answers cite `^[source.md:42-58]` with line ranges.
- **`hybrid`** — Combine both. Wiki pages rank higher but raw sources complement when no wiki page exists.

**Implementation:**
- Each scope maintains a separate search index (or separate index partitions)
- `wiki` searches the compiled article index (FTS5 + vectors)
- `raw` searches the source document index (FTS5 + vectors on source chunks)
- `hybrid` runs both in parallel, merges via RRF, wiki results get ×1.5 boost
- Scope indicator in output: `[wiki] attention` vs `[raw] transformer-paper.pdf`

**How to test:**
- Compile a wiki from test sources
- Test `--scope wiki` returns only wiki page results
- Test `--scope raw` returns only source document results
- Test `--scope hybrid` returns both, with wiki results ranked higher
- Test with a query that has no wiki match but has raw match (verify hybrid falls back)
- Test with a query that has no raw match but has wiki match
- Test `--top-k` limits results in all scopes
- Test default scope is hybrid
- Integration test: add source → compile → query wiki scope → verify answer cites wiki → query raw scope → verify answer cites source

**What to document:**
- `docs/guides/query.md`: scope descriptions, when to use each
- CLI `--help` for `knox query` (new `--scope` flag)
- FAQ: "What's the difference between wiki and raw search?"

title: N5: Web UI (dashboard, graph, drag-and-drop ingest)
description:
Add a web UI for browsing, searching, and managing the compiled wiki without a terminal.

**Design:**

A lightweight local web server (similar to `llmwiki view` or NiharShrotri's web UI):

```bash
knox serve                   # Start web UI at http://127.0.0.1:8765
knox serve --port 8080       # Custom port
knox serve --open            # Open browser automatically
```

**Pages:**
- **Dashboard** — project stats: source count, article count, last compile time, health score (N2), recent activity
- **Sources** — list of indexed sources with metadata (format, hash, last compile)
- **Wiki** — browseable compiled pages with sidebar navigation, full-text search
- **Query** — chat-style Q&A interface against the wiki (drives `knox query` backend)
- **Graph** — D3 force-directed visualization of the wiki: pages as nodes, `[[wikilinks]]` as edges, color-coded by page type
- **Ingest** — drag-and-drop file upload, URL paste, live progress log
- **Jobs** — history of all ingest/compile runs with progress bars
- **Lint** — interactive lint report with one-click auto-fix
- **Settings** — view effective config, LLM status, storage stats

**Technical approach:**
- Python-based: FastAPI backend + plain HTML/CSS/JS frontend (no Node build step)
- Or: embed a preact/svelte SPA via `importlib.resources`
- Reads directly from the compiled wiki on disk (no database dependency)
- Server is read-only for wiki browsing; write operations go through CLI commands
- Private by default: binds to `127.0.0.1` only

**How to test:**
- Start server on an empty project → verify dashboard shows zero counts
- Start server after compile → verify wiki pages render with correct markdown
- Test sidebar navigation across page types
- Test full-text search returns expected results
- Test graph visualization: create pages with wikilinks → verify graph shows connections
- Test drag-and-drop ingest: upload a PDF → verify source appears and triggers compile
- Test job history: run compile → verify job appears with status + duration
- Test lint UI: run lint → verify interactive report with one-click fix
- Test `--open` flag opens default browser
- Test server binding (127.0.0.1 only by default, `--host 0.0.0.0` allowed with warning)

**What to document:**
- `docs/guides/web-ui.md`: setup, screenshots, feature tour
- `docs/guides/web-ui.md`: keyboard shortcuts, browser compatibility
- CLI `--help` for `knox serve`
- FAQ: "Can I access the web UI remotely?" (yes, with `--host 0.0.0.0 --allow-lan`)
- Security note: web UI is read-only by default; write operations require confirmation

title: Q22: learn/capture + ingest commands (knowledge injection)
description:
Add MCP tools + CLI commands for injecting knowledge from AI conversations or text snippets into the wiki.

**Problem:** When you discover something useful during an AI conversation (a decision, a gotcha, a reference), there's no easy way to inject that knowledge into the wiki without manually creating a source file and re-compiling.

**Design:**

**MCP tools:**
- `wiki_capture(text)` — Extracts knowledge items (decisions, discoveries, corrections) from conversation text via LLM, filters noise (greetings, retries, dead ends), writes them as source files, and queues compile
- `wiki_learn(text)` — Stores a single fact/snippet directly as a source file without LLM extraction

**CLI commands:**
```bash
knox capture "We decided to use QKV projections with RoPE for the attention mechanism"
knox learn  "The transformer paper uses d_model=512 and h=8 attention heads"
knox capture --file session-transcript.md        # Extract from a saved transcript
knox learn  --tag "literature" --tag "attention" # With tags for classification
```

**CLI ingestion commands:**
```bash
knox ingest https://arxiv.org/pdf/1234.56789     # Download + register + compile
knox ingest notes/meeting-notes.md               # Register local file + compile
```

**Workflow:**
1. During an AI session, user says "Save this to my wiki"
2. Agent calls `wiki_capture` MCP tool with relevant text
3. Tool extracts structured knowledge items
4. Each item is written as a source file in `sources/_captured/` with YAML frontmatter
5. Items are queued for next compile
6. `knox compile` picks up new source files automatically

**Prior art:** `sage-wiki` `learn`/`capture`/`ingest`/`add-source` commands, `sage-wiki` scribe system, `claude-code` project knowledge

**Acceptance criteria:**
- `wiki_capture` MCP tool accepts a text string, returns list of extracted items with metadata
- `wiki_learn` MCP tool accepts a text string, writes a single source file
- Noise filtering: greetings, retries, dead ends excluded
- Captured sources go to `sources/_captured/` with structured frontmatter
- `knox capture` CLI wraps the MCP tool for non-MCP usage
- `knox learn` CLI stores a single fact as a `.md` source file
- `knox ingest` downloads and registers URLs as sources
- Sources dir changes are detected on next compile (manifest hash)
- New tests: capture output schema, noise filtering, ingest of local files

title: Q25: Search quality enhancements (chunk index, query expansion, re-ranking, graph context)
description:
Enhance `knox query` with multi-stage retrieval for higher accuracy: chunk-level indexing, LLM query expansion, hybrid BM25+vector search, cross-lingual support, LLM re-ranking, and graph-enhanced context.

**Phase 1 — Chunk-level indexing**
Instead of indexing at the article level, index individual chunks (already produced by HybridChunker). Each chunk gets:
- FTS5 full-text entry (for BM25 keyword search)
- Vector embedding (for cosine similarity search)
- Metadata: source article, section heading, position

**Phase 2 — Hybrid BM25 + vector search**
```yaml
search:
  hybrid_weight_bm25: 0.7
  hybrid_weight_vector: 0.3
  default_limit: 10
```
RRF (Reciprocal Rank Fusion) to combine BM25 and vector scores.

**Phase 3 — LLM Query Expansion**
Before searching, ask the LLM to generate:
- Keyword rewrites (for BM25 recall)
- Semantic rewrites (for vector search recall)
- A hypothetical answer (HyDE — for embedding similarity)
Apply a strong-signal check: skip expansion if the top BM25 result is already confident.

**Phase 4 — Reliable Cross-Lingual Search**
Full brute-force cosine search across all chunk vectors + BM25 via RRF fusion. This ensures multilingual queries (e.g., Polish query against English content) find semantically relevant results even when zero lexical overlap exists.

**Phase 5 — LLM Re-Ranking**
Score top N candidates (default 15) by the LLM for relevance. Use position-aware blending to protect high-confidence retrieval results:
- Ranks 1-3: 75% retrieval weight, 25% reranker
- Ranks 4-10: 50/50 blend
- Ranks 11+: 40% retrieval, 60% reranker

**Phase 6 — Graph-Enhanced Context**
After retrieval, expand context using the ontology graph with a 4-signal scorer:
- Direct relations (×3.0) — articles directly connected to retrieved articles
- Shared source documents (×4.0) — articles from the same source
- Common neighbors via Adamic-Adar (×1.5) — articles linked to the same intermediate concept
- Entity type affinity (×1.0) — same entity type bonus

```yaml
search:
  graph_expansion: true
  graph_max_expand: 10
  graph_depth: 2
  weight_direct_link: 3.0
  weight_source_overlap: 4.0
  weight_common_neighbor: 1.5
  weight_type_affinity: 1.0
```

**Prior art:** `sage-wiki` search quality system (inspired by qmd analysis)

**Acceptance criteria (incremental — each phase independently testable):**
- Phase 1: chunks stored in FTS5 + vector index; search returns chunk-level results
- Phase 2: hybrid BM25+vector with configurable weights; RRF fusion implemented
- Phase 3: LLM query expansion generates + uses rewrites; strong-signal skip works
- Phase 4: cross-lingual query finds semantically relevant results even with zero BM25 matches
- Phase 5: re-ranker scores top-N candidates; position-aware blending protects top ranks
- Phase 6: graph expansion adds related articles; 4-signal scorer weights configurable
- Each phase: existing lower phases continue to work (backwards compat)
- Phase 6: benchmark recall@10 >= 90% on known corpus
- Config-driven: each phase can be toggled on/off individually
notes:
## Improvements from Research (audit 2026-06-07)

### 1. Parent-child chunking (from WeKnora)
Add hierarchical chunking strategy: parent chunks (section-level) contain child
chunks (paragraph-level). Search returns child chunks with parent context,
improving retrieval relevance. Configurable via chunk_strategy: flat | parent-child.

### 2. Multiple configurable retrieval strategies (from WeKnora)
Instead of a fixed hybrid search, allow per-knowledge-base or per-query selection:
- bm25 — keyword-only (fast, free)
- dense — vector-only (semantic)
- hybrid — BM25 + vector RRF (default)
- graphrag — graph-enhanced retrieval
- multi-dim — multi-dimensional indexing

### 3. Progress callbacks for indexing (from qmd)

onProgress callback with (current, total, phase, eta) for both CLI progress bars
and programmatic API consumers.

### 4. Typed sub-queries (from qmd)
Replace single hybrid-weight with typed sub-queries:
- lex: keyword (BM25) query
- vec: semantic (vector) query
- hyde: hypothetical answer embedding
Combined via RRF with per-type weights. The original query gets ×2 weight.

title: Q24: Contribution packs (domain-specific ontology + prompts)
description:
A pack system that bundles ontology types, prompts, sample sources, and parser config for specific domains — installable as composable units.

**Problem:** The KNOX pipeline's quality depends heavily on good prompts, a well-tuned ontology, and sensible defaults. These vary by domain: a medical paper needs `contradicts` and `trial_phase` relations; a software project needs `implements` and `depends_on`. Rather than asking every user to tune these from scratch, offer pre-built packs.

**Design:**

A pack is a directory with this structure:

```
my-pack/
├── pack.yaml              # metadata: name, version, description, author
├── ontology.yaml          # entity_types, relation_types (merged with existing)
├── prompts/
│   ├── summarize-article.md    # template overrides
│   ├── write-article.md
│   ├── extract-concepts.md
│   └── caption-image.md
├── samples/               # optional sample sources for demos
│   └── sample-paper.pdf
├── parsers/               # optional external parser defs
│   └── rtf.yaml
└── config.yaml            # optional defaults (chunk_size, tier_defaults, etc.)
```

**CLI:**

```bash
# Browse
knox pack list                           # installed packs
knox pack search "medical"               # search registry (TODO: remote registry?)
knox pack info academic-research          # show pack details

# Install
knox pack install academic-research       # bundled pack
knox pack install https://github.com/user/my-pack.git   # git URL

# Apply (merge into project)
knox pack apply academic-research --mode merge     # union-merge with existing config
knox pack apply academic-research --mode replace   # replace existing config
knox pack validate                              # validate all applied pack configs

# Manage
knox pack remove academic-research              # un-apply
knox pack update [name]                         # check for updates
knox pack conflicts                              # show multi-pack file overlaps
```

**Merge strategy:**
- `ontology.yaml` — entity_types and relation_types are union-merged; synonyms appended
- `prompts/` — files are added; existing files are NOT overwritten without `--force`
- Conflicts (two packs providing the same prompt file) are reported by `knox pack conflicts`
- `parsers/` — external parser defs are added to the parser registry
- `config.yaml` — scoped defaults; per-pack values don't override user's config.yaml

**Bundled packs to ship initially:**
- `academic-research` — `cites`, `contradicts`, `finding`, `hypothesis`; WiCER prompts for papers
- `software-engineering` — `implements`, `depends_on`, `adr`, `runbook`; prompts for technical docs
- `personal-knowledge` — `relates_to`, `inspired_by`; simpler prompts for notes

**Prior art:** `sage-wiki` contribution packs (8 bundled), VSCode extensions, Obsidian community themes

**Acceptance criteria:**
- `knox pack install` from local path and git URL
- `knox pack apply --mode merge` merges ontology types (no duplicates)
- `knox pack apply --mode replace` overwrites with pack's version
- `knox pack remove` reverts the merge
- Prompt files are written to `prompts/` directory
- `knox pack conflicts` shows overlapping files between applied packs
- `knox pack validate` checks pack schema (required fields, valid YAML)
- Bundled packs work offline (no network needed for built-in packs)
- All existing tests pass with no packs applied
notes:
## Improvements from Research (audit 2026-06-07)

### 1. Role packs (from anh-chu)
Packs can include role personas (PM, researcher, executive, founder) that tune:
- Recall sensitivity (how aggressively to surface related content)
- Output format (brevity vs depth, markdown vs structured)
- Template selection (which crystallize pattern to use)
- Proactive trigger sensitivity (when the pack prompts without being asked)

### 2. Template-based rendering (from notebooklm-llm-wiki-flow)
Instead of code-based output writers, use Jinja2 templates for page rendering.
Each pack ships templates/ directory with:
- entity.md.j2, concept.md.j2, comparison.md.j2
- crystallize-digest.md.j2
- index.md.j2, log.md.j2
Users can override templates in their project or pack without touching Python code.

### 3. Sub-skills as composable units (from anh-chu)
Packs can declare sub-skills that are optionally installed:
- llm-wiki-pm/brief — daily/weekly briefs
- llm-wiki-pm/prd — PRD drafts, user stories
- llm-wiki-pm/research — research sprints, deep dives
- llm-wiki-pm/crm — relationship health tracking

### 4. Schema-driven pack extension (N9)
Each pack can extend the base schema with domain-specific page kinds.
The academic-research pack would add finding, hypothesis, experiment kinds.

### Testing
- Unit test: role pack merges correctly with base pack config
- Unit test: Jinja2 template renders with mock data
- Unit test: template overrides take precedence over built-in templates
- Integration test: apply academic pack → compile → verify finding pages produced
- Integration test: apply two packs with overlapping kinds → union merge
- Integration test: sub-skill install/remove lifecycle

### Documentation
- docs/guides/packs.md: role packs reference, schema extension
- docs/guides/packs.md: writing custom templates (Jinja2 guide)
- docs/guides/packs.md: sub-skill distribution pattern
- CLI --help for knox pack (new flags: --role, --sub-skill)
- Tutorial: "Creating a domain pack with custom page kinds"
- Tutorial: "Building a PM workflow with role packs and sub-skills"
